questions.question: Why was brute-force enumeration of stoichiometric c-LLZO configurations infeasible, and what was the initial combinatorial count?

options.A: Populating 120 sites with 56 Li gives about 7.4×10^34 arrangements
options.B: Populating 56 sites with 120 Li gives 2.3×10^8 arrangements
options.C: There are only 120 possible arrangements, but each requires a full geometry optimization
options.D: The count is 2×10^6 because all configurations are already symmetry unique

questions.rationale: The enormous raw occupancy count motivated geometric and symmetry-based pruning before energy ranking.
questions.evidence_quote: The number of ways to populate 120 sites with 56 Li is 120 56 ≈ 7.4 × 10 34 , rendering a brute-force combinatorial method unviable.

questions.question: What does the 1.7 Å Li–Li exclusion constraint imply for the partially occupied 96h sites?

options.A: At most 48 of the paired 96h sites can be occupied, and each occupied 24d site excludes four 96h sites
options.B: All 96h sites can be occupied if no 24d site is occupied
options.C: Each 24d site excludes exactly one 96h site, allowing 56 total Li on 96h
options.D: The constraint eliminates every 24d site and leaves 24 occupied 96h sites

questions.rationale: Each 96h pair is only 0.68 Å apart, and the stated cutoff also excludes neighboring 96h sites around an occupied 24d position.
questions.evidence_quote:
1. A maximum of 48 out of 96h sites can be occupied at anyone time: each 96h site exists as a pair within 0.68 Å of each other, at most one site can contain a Li atom.
2. Each of the 24d occupation eliminates 4 out of 96h sites as they are within 1.67 Å of this site.

questions.question: How did the structure-generation stage avoid forbidden nearest-neighbor Li overlaps?

options.A: It enumerated 24d permutations first, removed adjacent 96h candidates, then filled 96h without simultaneous nearest-neighbor occupation
options.B: It placed all 96h Li randomly and relaxed overlaps with molecular dynamics
options.C: It generated only the 48g site and inferred the 24d/96h occupancies afterward
options.D: It used diffraction intensities to choose one experimentally observed configuration

questions.rationale: The procedure applies the geometric constraint during enumeration, before symmetry reduction.
questions.evidence_quote: We initially generate all possible 24d permutations for a given 24d occupancy, eliminating directly neighbouring 96h sites from consideration. We then populate the remaining 96h sites such that no two nearest neighbours are occupied simultaneously.

questions.question: What representation and search method were used to reduce symmetry-equivalent configurations efficiently?

options.A: A sorted flattened upper-triangular Li–Li distance matrix with local sensitive hashing
options.B: A full Cartesian-coordinate comparison of every pair using conventional O(N²) search
options.C: A reciprocal-space diffraction fingerprint with principal-component analysis
options.D: A La–Zr interaction matrix ranked by a neural network

questions.rationale: The Li sublattice connectivity matrix stores pairwise distances, and LSH accelerates the approximate symmetry similarity searches.
questions.evidence_quote: To further reduce our large data set to unique conformations, we construct the upper triangular connectivity matrix of the Li sub-lattice for each structure. We define a connectivity matrix as the distances between each Li atom to every other Li atom. The matrix is then flattened and sorted to ensure uniformity in all matrices.

questions.question: What were the scale and trade-off of the local-sensitive-hashing symmetry reduction?

options.A: It reduced pairwise scaling from O(N²) to O(N), but its high specificity trades away some completeness
options.B: It reduced O(N) to O(N²), improving sensitivity at the cost of memory
options.C: It guaranteed exact symmetry for arbitrary atomic species with no approximation
options.D: It only worked for 20 structures and did not reduce memory

questions.rationale: The method is fast and memory efficient for large similar datasets but is approximate/high-specificity and limited to predefined monoatomic sublattices.
questions.evidence_quote:
The use of LSH optimises the pairwise comparison from scaling at
O(N 2 ) to O(N ),
where N is the number of structures. This symmetry comparison method is designed to work for large data sets of similar data, allowing us to perform symmetry checks on over 100 million structures in a reasonable time frame and attainable memory requirements, something that would be impractical to attempt with conventional methods. [48] [49] [50] The trade-off for increased speed and lower memory costs is the high specificity of the method.
In practice, this method is limited to comparison of monoatomic sub-lattices with predefined positions.

questions.question: How many configurations remained after the two main reductions, and what fraction were symmetry unique?

options.A: About 1% were unique, leaving roughly 2×10^6 configurations from an initial 2.3×10^8
options.B: About 99% were unique, leaving 2.3×10^8 configurations from 2×10^6
options.D: The configuration count was unchanged because symmetry duplicates were retained

questions.rationale: The geometric enumeration yielded around 230 million structures, and symmetry hashing reduced them by about a factor of 100.
questions.evidence_quote: This method will generate all possible structures, approximately 2.3 × 10 8 , including symmetry-equivalent duplicates.

questions.question: How were the DFT training structures selected for the multiple-linear-regression energy model?

options.A: The 200 lowest COMPASSIII structures plus about 1,000 random structures spanning the space, for 1,235 DFT points total
options.B: The 1,235 lowest-energy structures according to ONETEP only
options.C: A random sample of 200 structures, all from the 8:48 ratio
options.D: Every one of the approximately two million structures received a DFT calculation

questions.rationale: The two subsets combine a low-energy-biased sample and broad random coverage to train an energy predictor affordably.
questions.evidence_quote: The DFT calculations were performed on 2 major subsets of structures. The first subset was the 200 energetically lowest structures according to the COMPASSIII forcefield, 51 (c.f. SI section ). The second subset was a random selection of approximately 1000 structures across the entire configuration space to ensure good coverage. In total 1235 single point DFT calculations were performed.

questions.question: What descriptor did the MLR model use, and how well did it correlate with held-out DFT energies?

options.A: Frequencies of possible Li–Li interactions, with a test-set correlation of 0.9996
options.C: Total Li count and lattice volume, with correlation 0.83
options.D: A neural embedding of La/Zr sites, with correlation 0.58

questions.rationale: The pair-interaction frequency list reformulates the Li connectivity matrix and was strongly predictive on the held-out set.
questions.evidence_quote:
The structures were represented by a frequency occurrence list of all possible Li-Li interactions.
This representation is a reformulation of the connectivity matrix of the Li sub-lattice used for the symmetry reduction described above. The data were split into test and training sets with a 1:3 ratio.
We found through applying this model to our test set a correlation of 0.9996

questions.question: What occupancy pattern dominated the low-energy structures, and what energetic separation did the authors report?

options.A: Nineteen of the 20 lowest were 8:48, with four such structures within 0.026 eV of the minimum
options.B: Nineteen of the 20 lowest were 12:44, all separated by over 1.47 eV
options.C: The 9:47 ratio dominated and was 0.58 eV below all 8:48 structures
options.D: All ratios were equally represented within 5.8 meV

questions.rationale: The low-energy ranking strongly favors low 24d occupation and identifies four near-degenerate 8:48 structures.
questions.evidence_quote: 19 out of the 20 lowest energy structures have a ratio of 8:48 (c.f. Figure 2b ) with the 19 th lowest being 9:47. The average energy for all structures occurs at 1.47 eV higher than the ground state structures. The average energy for each ratio increases with increasing 24d occupancy, indicating an energetic preference to avoid 24d occupation where possible. There are four structures, all 8:48, within 0.026 eV (1 kT at 298 K) of the lowest energy structure we find

questions.question: Which limitations qualify the study's energetic ranking of candidate structures?

options.A: It omits entropic contributions and assumes ordering is reasonably retained under relaxation; only a small relaxation subset was tested
options.B: It includes full entropy but assumes the structure never relaxes
options.C: It optimizes all two million configurations and therefore has no model uncertainty
options.D: It uses only experimental energies and excludes geometric constraints

questions.rationale: The authors explicitly flag entropy and ordering retention as approximations and note that broad energy prediction after relaxation is outside scope.
questions.evidence_quote: We note that our energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions and assumes a reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation, which are both approximations. We have tested the effect of geometry relaxation on a small dataset of 20 structures (c.f. SI section ). A large-scale energy prediction of the geometry optimised structures falls outside the scope of this communication.
